historic_survey.note: Listed among the five designated San Francisco Landmarks in the study area, as Landmark #100, and named as the most prominent extant theatre in the district. The statement gives the address as 429 Castro Street where it lists the landmarks and describes the building, and as 429-431 in a figure caption. Its recommendations and a quotation from the citywide LGBTQ context statement instead attach Landmark #100 to 479 Castro Street — the parcel the statement elsewhere identifies as the site of the Nasser Brothers' theatre of 1910, this one's predecessor.

historical_record.description: The theatre anchored the northern end of the Castro Street commercial corridor, linking the commercial growth on Market Street to the major intersection of Castro and 18th streets.
The Castro Theater, designed by architect Timothy Pflueger.
Fire-insurance maps show a pair of apartment buildings and a garage on the site before the theatre was built.
Opened with 2,000 seats, at a cost of $300,000. Faggioni Studios did the interior decoration and the orchestral organ was a Robert Morton.

The theatre was revived as a repertory house catering to camp-attuned audiences. That revival, the founding of the Castro Street Fair in 1974 and the move of gay Halloween festivities from Polk Street and North Beach to the Castro in 1976 together solidified the neighbourhood's gay identity.
Reopened to the public after a two-year closure and a $41 million renovation that restored historic elements and added removable seating for concerts.
